description: Hi! We're Dharan & Akanksha, from the university of exeter MSc in Generative AI. We have around 2 years of experience as a Generative AI Engineer, working on building production-ready AI applications, LLM-based systems and AI agents.
summary:
Flame in Freefall is a web dashboard that reads NASA’s 24 microgravity fire experiments from the Physical Sciences Informatics repository and makes them easy to use. You can browse every experiment on one screen, rank them for a mission such as a moon base, compare them side by side, and find the real tests closest to conditions you choose. A gap map shows which oxygen and pressure conditions NASA has never tested. Four models and a droplet simulation estimate results between tested conditions and refuse to answer outside them. A question box and a voice guide explain any page in plain words.

Code reads every number from NASA’s tables and links it back to its source row. The AI layer explains the data and never produces a figure of its own.

This matters because Moon habitats are planned with 30% oxygen or more, which makes materials easier to ignite, and a crew cannot leave a fire. Our tool shows that no solid material has been tested in orbit above 22.2% oxygen.
details:
What it does and how it works

Flame in Freefall is a web dashboard built on NASA’s 24 microgravity combustion experiments from the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository. A script downloads the records and test tables from NASA’s open API and keeps them unchanged. Code then reads every table, converts the units, and flags cells that look wrong (70 of them) without editing NASA’s data.

The site has five sections. Experiments lists all 24 investigations, ranks them for a mission such as a moon base, compares them side by side, and finds the real tests nearest to conditions you type. Habitats maps the oxygen and pressure conditions that were never tested and suggests experiments to run next. Models predict droplet burning rate, flame self-extinction and gas-flame ignition inside the range NASA tested and refuse outside it. The lab simulates a burning droplet and plots the real tests. Ask questions with a source on every sentence. A voice guide explains any page aloud and takes questions.

Benefits and intended impact

A student gets the field explained in plain words, with a simulation to try. A researcher finds the relevant experiments and the exact table rows behind every number. Both can see what is missing: no solid material has been tested in orbit above 22.2% oxygen, while Moon habitats are planned at 30% or more. We want the gap map and its ranked suggestions to help decide which fire experiments fly next.

Tools

Python (FastAPI, pandas, scikit-learn) for the data pipeline, the models and the server. TypeScript and React for the website. A Qwen language model on Amazon Bedrock writes the summaries and explanations, and ElevenLabs provides the voice. We used GitHub, 221 automated tests, and AI-assisted coding with Claude Code. It runs on an ordinary laptop.

What is creative about it?

The AI never produces a number. Code computes every figure and rejects any AI sentence containing a number that is not in NASA’s data. The models give no answer when asked about untested conditions, and we checked one of them against a 1997 Spacelab experiment it had never seen. The voice guide can be interrupted mid-sentence, and it words its explanation for a student or for a researcher.

What we considered

We put trust first, so every value links to its NASA table, row and column. We kept NASA’s data unedited and labelled simulations as simulations. We marked Moon and Mars gravity as untested because no such data exists. We trained one model per fuel class, because droplets, gases and solids burn differently. It is a research and teaching aid, not a certified safety tool.
projectRefs: Amazon Bedrock (hosts the Qwen3 language model that writes summaries and explanations)
ElevenLabs Agents (voice guide: speech recognition and text to speech)
